intro.text: At the top of the city stands the Oracle, a machine that answers any question in a confident voice. Sometimes it is wrong in a confident voice.
Quack. AI is a tool, not an authority. Your job is to ask well and check what comes back.

mid.text: You can catch the Oracle's inventions. Now the other half: asking it well, and knowing how it works.
Quack. A few questions about how these models behave.

outro.text: The Oracle bows to a skeptic. You trust it only as far as you can verify it.
Quack. You have cleared Segfault City. Keep checking your work.

games.title: Catch the Hallucination
games.instructions: Each answer has exactly one invented claim. Click it.

claims: Python was created by Guido van Rossum.
Its first public release came in 1991.
It was developed at Google and first released in 2015.
Python uses indentation to define code blocks.
rounds.why: Invented. Python came from Guido van Rossum and first appeared in 1991, long before 2015, and not as a Google project.

rounds.prompt: Tell me about the C language.
claims: C was developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs.
It was created in the early 1970s.
C was designed in part to write the Unix operating system.
C has automatic garbage collection built in.
rounds.why: Invented. C leaves memory management to you, which is why Week 4 had malloc and free.

rounds.prompt: What does research say about rubber duck debugging?
claims: Explaining code aloud can reveal bugs.
The technique is described in the book The Pragmatic Programmer.
A 2021 paper by Dr. A. Quill in the Journal of Imaginary Computing proved ducks cut bugs by 73%.
CS50 has its own debugging duck.
rounds.why: Invented. A very specific citation and a precise percentage are classic hallucination signs. Search for the paper before you trust it.

rounds.q: Which prompt is most likely to get a useful answer?
options: Here is my code and the exact error. Explain what is wrong without giving me the full solution.
rounds.explain: Context, the exact error, and a clear request for the kind of help you want.

rounds.q: Why can a language model state false facts confidently?
options: It looks facts up in a verified database
It predicts likely next words, which is not the same as checking facts
It only repeats its last answer
rounds.explain: Models generate plausible text. Plausible is not the same as true.

options: Text in the input that tricks a model into ignoring its original instructions
A way to speed up responses
rounds.explain: Instructions hidden in user input or a web page can hijack a model. Treat outside text as untrusted.

rounds.q: AI hands you code you don't understand. What's the best habit?
options: Paste it in and move on
Ask it to explain, then run tests and verify the behaviour yourself
Delete it and never use AI
Assume it is correct if it compiles
rounds.explain: Understanding and testing are your responsibility, whoever wrote the code.
